title: MYP Interdisciplinary Learning Criteria Explained
summary: MYP Interdisciplinary Learning criteria explained through teacher feedback, with high-band examples and a clear guide to current A-C and older A-D rubrics.
body_markdown:
A student opens their teacher’s feedback and finds a familiar frustration: the project contains plenty of research, but the comments ask for stronger connections. What, exactly, is missing?


The **MYP Interdisciplinary Learning criteria** assess how students use knowledge from different subjects to develop understanding that one subject alone would not provide. There is one essential clarification before interpreting the feedback: **the current interdisciplinary framework uses three criteria, A-C. The older framework used four, A-D.** Their letters do not always mean the same thing.


This guide follows a hypothetical student revising a project about access to clean drinking water, combining Sciences with Individuals and Societies. It explains the current criteria first, then maps the older A-D rubric so students and parents can recognize both.


### Check which MYP Interdisciplinary Learning rubric you have


Start with the criterion names printed on the assignment sheet.


Framework Criterion A Criterion B Criterion C Criterion D


Current framework, introduced in the 2021 guide Evaluating Synthesizing Reflecting No separate criterion D


Older framework Disciplinary grounding Synthesizing Communicating Reflecting


In the current framework, each criterion has a maximum achievement level of 8. The descriptor bands are 1-2, 3-4, 5-6 and 7-8, with level 0 available when work does not reach the described standards.


Before revising, check:


- Which framework and year-level descriptors does the teacher’s rubric use?
- Which subjects contribute to the task?
- What product or response must you submit?
- Where must you explain your thinking and reflect on learning?


The[overview of MYP subject groups](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/what-are-myp-subject-groups) helps parents understand the disciplines involved. Use the teacher’s task-specific clarifications alongside the rubric when deciding what evidence to include.


### MYP Interdisciplinary Learning criterion A: Evaluating


Imagine the student’s teacher writes: “You have included scientific facts and social information. Explain what each perspective contributes and where it has limitations.”


Criterion A asks students to analyse disciplinary knowledge and evaluate interdisciplinary perspectives. In plain language: understand the subjects, explain their contributions, and judge the strengths and limitations of the perspectives being brought together.


For the drinking-water project, Sciences might explain contamination and treatment. Individuals and Societies might examine infrastructure, affordability and decision-making. Accurate information matters, but simply placing it in adjacent paragraphs leaves the relationship unexplained.


### What a high-band response looks like


A response working towards the 7-8 band gives developed explanations. It might explain that testing water quality helps identify a health risk, while investigating household income helps assess whether a proposed treatment is accessible.


It would also evaluate limitations. Laboratory evidence alone cannot establish whether families can afford a filter. Interviews about affordability cannot establish whether that filter removes a particular contaminant.


The revision question is: **What can each discipline help me understand, and what remains unresolved?**


For more context on these connections, explore[subjects that pair with MYP Individuals and Societies](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/subjects-that-pair-with-myp-individuals-and-societies) .


A student presents a tangled ball of string as two teachers ask for an explanation of the connections.


### Criterion B: Synthesizing


The next hypothetical comment reads: “Your recommendation uses both subjects. Show why combining them changes your conclusion.”


Synthesis means bringing disciplinary knowledge together to create a purposeful interdisciplinary understanding. Under the current rubric, students create a product that communicates that understanding and justify how the product does so.


A product could take different forms depending on the assignment. Whatever its format, its purpose should guide the connections.


### What a high-band response looks like


Suppose the student recommends a community water-treatment approach. The recommendation draws on evidence about effectiveness alongside evidence about cost, maintenance and local access. Those considerations work together to shape the decision.


The student then justifies the product’s choices. For example, a comparison chart places treatment performance beside ongoing costs because the intended audience needs both to judge feasibility.


A useful revision test is: **If I removed either subject, would my conclusion become weaker or change?** If neither happens, the work may need a clearer connection.


The[guide to interdisciplinary learning in Individuals and Societies](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/individuals-and-societies-interdisciplinary-learning-explained) offers further context for combining social perspectives with other disciplines.


### Criterion C: Reflecting


The final comment says: “Explain how your understanding developed and how it could inform action.”


Current criterion C concerns reflection. Students discuss the development of their interdisciplinary learning and how their new understanding enables action.


A reflection that only recounts the work completed gives the teacher little evidence of intellectual development. A stronger reflection identifies a change in understanding and explains what caused it.


### What a high-band response looks like


The student might explain that they initially judged water-treatment options mainly by scientific effectiveness. Research into maintenance and affordability then changed the recommendation. They identify the evidence that prompted that change and discuss its implications.


For action, they could explain how the combined understanding would help them develop questions for a community consultation or evaluate a proposed school water initiative. Keep the discussion realistic and connected to the learning.


A useful writing scaffold is: **I initially thought… Evidence from… changed my understanding because… This could inform…** Develop each part with specific examples from your work.


### What the older A-D criteria mean


If your assignment uses four interdisciplinary criteria, the following explanations will help you read the feedback. These are plain-language summaries, not replacements for the supplied descriptors.


Older criterion What it assesses What a strong response demonstrates


A: Disciplinary grounding The subject knowledge and methods supporting the work Relevant, accurate disciplinary understanding used effectively for the inquiry


B: Synthesizing How disciplinary contributions combine A clear explanation of how integration advances interdisciplinary understanding


C: Communicating How understanding is presented Appropriate structure, disciplinary communication choices and documentation of sources


D: Reflecting How the student evaluates interdisciplinary learning A reasoned discussion of learning development, benefits and limitations


The important distinction is criterion C: **Communicating in the older framework becomes Reflecting in the current framework.** Current criterion A also goes beyond the older label of disciplinary grounding by explicitly requiring evaluation.


Avoid borrowing a rubric from an unrelated subject. As the[guide to MYP criteria A, B, C and D](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/myp-criteria-a-b-c-d-explained) illustrates, criterion letters have different meanings across MYP assessment contexts.


### Turn feedback into a focused revision plan


Our hypothetical student now has three manageable actions: explain each discipline’s contribution, strengthen the reasoning behind the combined recommendation, and show how their understanding changed.


Parents can support this process by asking the student to locate evidence for each descriptor. “Which paragraph shows that?” often produces a more useful conversation than asking how many marks the project will receive.

The student’s next draft should make their thinking easier to see: what each subject contributes, what their combination makes possible, and how that understanding developed. That is the thread connecting useful feedback to better interdisciplinary work.
